title: Battery Pack Design: EV Worked Example (S/P, Heat) | Skill-Lync
summary: Battery pack design worked for a 40 kWh Indian EV: series and parallel cell count, mass, I²R heat, coolant flow, BMS, pre-charge and AIS-038 rules.
body_markdown:
Battery pack design turns a vehicle's targets (range, peak power and system voltage) into a cell count and a way of wiring the cells. The voltage window sets how many cells go in series. The energy and current the car needs set how many go in parallel. Then come the checks on mass, heat, cooling and protection, and in India the pack must meet AIS-038 (Rev 2) for cars or AIS-156 for two- and three-wheelers. Below, we design a 40 kWh, 350 V pack for a compact Indian EV from a real cell datasheet, with every number recomputed by script.


- **96S24P of Samsung INR21700-50E cells** (3.63 V, 4.9 Ah minimum, 69.5 g maximum; Samsung SDI specification, 2019): 2,304 cells, 348.5 V nominal (240 to 403.2 V), 40.98 kWh.
- **The 100 kW peak draws 287 A, or 11.96 A per cell.** That is above the cell's 9.8 A continuous rating but under its 14.7 A short-duration rating, so the peak must stay a pulse.
- **Cells weigh 160.1 kg and the pack about 252 kg** , if it matches the 63.4% cell-to-pack mass ratio TUM measured on a Volkswagen ID.3 (eTransportation, 2022).
- **Heat is 1.27 kW during a 1C charge and 7.58 kW at the peak** (23 mΩ per cell). The sustained charge sizes the cooling: about 7.2 L/min of 50% glycol for a 3 K rise.
- **Indian rules:** AIS-038 (Rev 2) Annexure IX-K, phased in on 1 Dec 2022 and 31 Mar 2023 (PIB, 27 Sep 2022), requires certified cells, a vent, an extra fuse or breaker, a BMS with five protections, IPX7 at full charge and a month of logged data.


## What are the steps in battery pack design?


Pack design is a chain of steps, each limiting the next: vehicle targets, then pack energy, cell choice, series count (S) and parallel count (P). After that come checks on mass, heat, cooling and electrical protection, and the standard the pack must pass. When a later check fails, the designer loops back, usually to the cell choice or P.


The example below runs this chain once. The[battery pack calculator](https://skill-lync.com/tools/battery-pack-calculator) repeats the S and P steps for any cell. Unit 21 of our[battery management systems book](https://skill-lync.com/books/battery-management-systems#unit-21-sizing) covers the same sizing in textbook form.


## How much energy does an EV battery pack need?


Pack energy is the promised range times the energy used per kilometre, divided by the share of cell energy the car may use. For 300 km of real-world range at 125 Wh/km with 93% usable, the pack needs 40.3 kWh. Consumption moves this answer most, so it should come from a drive-cycle model, not a guess.


Our targets are assumptions set close to compact EVs on sale in India. Tata's updated Punch.ev has a 40 kWh LFP pack and a claimed real-world range of about 355 km (Autocar Professional, 20 Feb 2026). That works out to 112.7 Wh of pack energy per km. We use 125 Wh/km, about 11% more, to leave margin for summer air-conditioning and ageing.

## What does a cell datasheet tell you for pack design?


The datasheet gives the voltage window, capacity, current ratings, mass, resistance and temperature limits that every later step divides by. Read the test conditions first. Capacity is often printed only as a minimum. Resistance is usually measured at AC 1 kHz, which understates the DC resistance that sets voltage sag and heat.


We use the Samsung INR21700-50E, a cylindrical cell 21 mm across and 70 mm long, because its full specification is public; automotive cell specifications are usually under NDA. It is a teaching choice, not a claim that any Indian car uses it.

**Use DC resistance for heat.** LG's comparable 21700 (INR21700-M50LT, 2020 tentative sheet) lists 15 ± 6 mΩ at AC 1 kHz but 23 ± 6 mΩ DC (0.5C, 10 s pulse, 50% charge). EVE's LF105 LFP cell shows the same gap: 0.32 mΩ AC against a DC limit of 1.8 mΩ. We take 23 mΩ as the 50E's DC design value and show the 14 mΩ AC result beside it; a real programme would measure it with a pulse test. The[battery cell comparison](https://skill-lync.com/tools/battery-cell-comparison) puts this cell beside 19 others, and Unit 3 of the[BMS book](https://skill-lync.com/books/battery-management-systems#unit-3-datasheet) explains each datasheet line.


## How do you calculate the number of cells in series?


Use enough cells in series that the pack stays above the drive's minimum voltage with every cell empty, and few enough that it stays below the maximum with every cell full. For a 230 to 420 V system and a 2.5 to 4.2 V cell, that allows 92 to 100 cells. We pick 96S: 348.5 V nominal, 240 to 403.2 V.

Every count from 92S to 100S keeps the full cell window inside the assumed 230 to 420 V system window. Figure: Skill-Lync, from the 50E datasheet limits.


Why 96 within that range? It leaves 16.8 V of margin below 420 V for measurement error and charger overshoot. It keeps more margin above the inverter's minimum when the cells sag under load at low charge. And 96 = 8 × 12: a 12S module peaks at 50.4 V, under the 60 V extra-low-voltage limit. The ID.3 uses the same 12-cell split so its modules need fewer touch-safety precautions.


## How do you calculate the number of cells in parallel?


The parallel count must store the energy and share the current so no cell exceeds its rating. Energy needs 40,323 / (96 × 17.787) = 23.61, rounded up to 24 cells per group. At the 100 kW peak each of those cells carries 11.96 A, inside its 14.7 A short-duration rating. So 24P works, provided the peak stays a pulse.

- **Continuous rating (9.8 A).** Carrying 287 A continuously would need 287 / 9.8 = 29.3, so 30P, a pack 25% larger than the energy needs. At 24P the continuous limit is 235.2 A, about 82.0 kW, enough for any sustained climb in a compact car.
- **Short-duration rating (14.7 A).** 24 cells allow 352.8 A in bursts, so the full 100 kW holds while the pack is above 283.4 V, or 2.95 V per cell under load. At the 240 V cut-off the same current gives only 84.7 kW, which is why the BMS limits power at low charge.
- **Charging.** The 4.9 A maximum gives 117.6 A, about 41.0 kW, and Samsung warns it is "not for cycle life". The 2.45 A standard charge gives 58.8 A, about 20.5 kW. A car promising faster DC charging needs a cell rated for higher charge current.


The peak also drops each cell by 11.96 × 0.023 = 0.275 V, which is 26.4 V across the pack. The BMS's state-of-power estimate has to allow for that sag.

The 1C figure (39.75 kWh) is below the 40.3 kWh target. Highway currents are well under 1C, so the pack delivers close to the 0.2C figure in normal driving. If the range promise had to hold at 1C, the next step would be 25P.


## How heavy is the battery pack, and do you need modules?


The cells weigh 2,304 × 69.5 g = 160.1 kg. Housing, cooling plates, busbars, BMS and fasteners add the rest. At the 63.4% cell-to-pack mass ratio measured on the ID.3, the pack weighs about 252 kg: 162 Wh/kg at pack level against 255.9 Wh/kg for the bare cell.


TUM's teardown of the ID.3 found 216 cells of 1.101 kg (237.8 kg) in a 375 kg pack including coolant, so 237.8 / 375 = 63.4%. Module hardware was 15% of each module's mass, and everything outside the modules was 26% of the pack. Removing that layer is the idea behind cell-to-pack designs. BYD's Blade Battery puts cells "in an array" straight into the pack and, BYD says, raises space utilisation by over 50% compared with conventional LFP block packs (29 Mar 2020); that is a volume claim, not mass.


Modules still have advantages. Each of our 12S24P modules stays at 50.4 V maximum, so it is safer to handle, can be tested before final assembly, and can be replaced on its own. Cell-to-pack saves mass and space but makes repair harder and leans on the pack structure to stop one cell's failure spreading. The S and P are the same either way.

The 7.58 kW peak does not size the cooling, because the cells' own heat capacity soaks up short pulses. At about 980 J/(kg K), measured on an NMC cylindrical cell (Bryden et al., 2018), one cell stores 68.1 J per kelvin. A 10 s peak puts 32.9 J into each cell, a 0.48 K rise. An hour of 1C charging puts in 1,988 J, a 29.2 K rise if nothing removes it. Starting from a 35 °C afternoon, that ends far above the 45 °C charging limit.


So sustained load (fast charging, long climbs, repeated hard driving) is the cooling design case, and the peak is a short thermal-mass check. Reversible (entropic) heat and busbar losses are left out here. Our post on[heat generation in battery packs](https://skill-lync.com/blogs/electrical-battery-packed-heat-generation) explains where cell heat comes from. The[battery thermal model calculator](https://skill-lync.com/tools/battery-thermal-model-calculator) runs the lumped-mass model over a drive.

The glycol values are Dow's tables for a 50% (by volume) solution at 30 °C: 3.321 kJ/(kg K) and 1,069.9 kg/m³. Air is 1.006 kJ/(kg K) and 1.146 kg/m³ at 35 °C. The 3 K and 10 K rises are our choices; a bigger rise means less flow but a wider temperature spread across the pack.


In India, ambient temperature can decide the method on its own. IMD declares a heatwave when the maximum reaches 45 °C, which is also this cell's upper charging limit. Air, or coolant cooled only by a radiator, cannot bring cells below the outside air. So a pack that fast-charges in a heatwave needs a refrigerant loop, a chiller on the car's AC circuit, to cool the coolant below ambient. Samsung also caps discharge at 70 °C cell surface. Our post on[battery thermal management systems](https://skill-lync.com/blogs/the-importance-of-battery-thermal-management-systems-in-electric-vehicles) compares air, liquid, refrigerant and phase-change cooling.


## What does the BMS, pre-charge, fuse and isolation design involve?


The BMS measures every series group's voltage, the pack current and enough temperatures to catch hot spots. From these it estimates state of charge, health and available power, balances the groups and opens the contactors when a limit is crossed. Our pack needs 96 voltage channels, one per 24-cell group, because cells in parallel share one voltage.


Balancing exists because small capacity and self-discharge differences let some groups reach 4.2 V first; passive balancing bleeds them through resistors, active balancing moves their charge to the low groups. Our post on[how a BMS works](https://skill-lync.com/blogs/how-does-a-battery-management-system-bms-work) covers SoC estimation and balancing with worked numbers.


The parts between the cells and the inverter. The BMS reads voltages, temperatures and current and drives the contactors; the isolation monitor watches both HV rails against the chassis.


### Why does a battery pack need a pre-charge circuit?


The inverter has a DC-link capacitor across its input, several hundred to thousands of microfarads according to TI. Closing the main contactors on it while empty is effectively a short circuit, and the inrush can damage cables, connectors and fuses. So the main negative contactor and a pre-charge contactor with a resistor close first. When the capacitor is near pack voltage, the main positive contactor closes and the pre-charge path opens. Charging a capacitor from a fixed voltage through a resistor burns as much energy in the resistor as ends up in the capacitor, so the resistor takes an 81 J pulse (541 W averaged over 150 ms; the link itself stores 73 J at 95%). That is a pulse, not a continuous load, so the resistor is chosen by its pulse rating.


### What fuses and isolation does the pack need?


AIS-038 (Rev 2) asks for a safety fuse or circuit breaker in addition to the BMS (Annexure IX-K, clause 7). For parallel strings it asks for active paralleling circuits, with fuses or bond wires as the alternative (clause 5). In a 24P pack the bond-wire option makes each cell's connection a small fuse, so a shorted cell is cut off instead of drawing current from its 23 neighbours. The main fuse must ride through the 287 A peak and 352.8 A pulses yet clear a short before cables and contactors are damaged.


The AIS-038 (Rev 2) finalized draft (ARAI, July 2020) sets the isolation between the HV DC bus and the chassis at 100 Ω per volt of working voltage. Where AC and DC buses are galvanically connected it is 500 Ω/V, unless the AC side is double-insulated or in robust housings (clauses 5.1.3.1 and 5.1.3.2). At our 403.2 V maximum, that is at least 40.3 kΩ, or 201.6 kΩ under the stricter rule. Unit 15 of the[BMS book](https://skill-lync.com/books/battery-management-systems#unit-15-hv) covers contactors, pre-charge, fuses and insulation monitoring together.


## What do AIS-038 (Rev 2) and AIS-156 require of an EV battery pack?


AIS-038 (Rev 2) covers cars, buses and trucks (M and N categories), and AIS-156 covers two- and three-wheelers (L category). After fires in electric two-wheelers, an expert committee recommended stricter battery rules and MoRTH amended both (PIB, 1 Sep 2022). Amendment 2 applied from 1 October 2022, and Amendment 3 came in two phases, on 1 December 2022 and 31 March 2023 (PIB, 27 Sep 2022). For a car pack, Annexure IX-K of AIS-038 (Rev 2) requires:


- **Cells:** manufacturing date (mm-yyyy) visible; certified to IS 16893 Parts 2 and 3; each put through at least one C/3 charge-discharge cycle, with the data kept.
- **Pack build:** a pressure-release vent; leak-proof coolant joints inside the battery; enough cell-to-cell spacing; protection against circulating currents in parallel strings; an extra fuse or breaker; protection of cells during regenerative braking.
- **Water:** no fire or explosion in an IPX7 test at 100% charge, or an ISO 6469-1:2019 immersion test.
- **BMS:** microcontroller-based; meets AIS 004 Part 3 for EMC; verified for over-charge, over-discharge, over-temperature, over-current and short-circuit protection; logs at least a month of data.
- **Charger and records:** cut-off, soft start, a deep-discharge check, 230 V AC ± 10% input protection, earth-leakage detection, BMS communication, and a traceability record for every pack.


The finalized draft, based on UN R100 Revision 3 and GTR 20, lists the pack type tests: vibration, thermal shock, mechanical impact, fire resistance, external short circuit, overcharge, over-discharge, over-temperature, overcurrent and low-temperature protection, plus gas management. It also requires a driver warning for a thermal event. If one cell's internal short sets off thermal propagation, the warning must come 5 minutes before any hazard reaches the cabin, unless propagation creates no hazard. We cite the finalized draft because ARAI's server for the published text did not respond.


AIS-156 for two-wheelers adds sensing rules: at least four temperature sensors per pack, with an alarm and a gradual power cut above 60 °C (Amendment 3, Annex 8K). Our explainer on[why EVs catch fire in India](https://skill-lync.com/blogs/why-do-electric-vehicles-catch-on-fire-in-india) covers the fires behind these rules.


## Would an LFP pack change the design?


Yes. LFP's lower voltage, lower energy per kilogram and large prismatic cells change the cell count and how finely you can size the pack. With EVE's 105 Ah LF105, 112 cells in series give 37.63 kWh at 358.4 V, 2.7 kWh short of target. The 420 V ceiling blocks more series cells, and going to 2P would halve the voltage.

Even at the 115S limit (419.75 V full) the LFP pack holds 38.64 kWh, so reaching 40.3 kWh means choosing a cell of a different capacity. The LF105 sheet's standard current is only 0.5C (52.5 A, about 18.8 kW); EV traction LFP cells are rated for more. Most compact EVs sold in India still take the LFP route, including the Punch.ev's 40 kWh pack and MG Windsor's 38 kWh pack (Autocar India, 11 Sep 2024). Our[LFP vs NMC comparison](https://skill-lync.com/blogs/lfp-vs-nmc-battery) explains why: cost, cycle life, heat tolerance, and the state-of-charge problem LFP's flat voltage curve creates.


## Where does this worked example simplify?


It shows the method, not a pack ready to build. The 50E is not sold as an automotive cell, and a car programme would use a qualified cell. We borrowed LG's DC resistance; real resistance rises with age and cold, so heat and sag at end of life are higher. We sized at the minimum capacity of a new cell, so 300 km after years of fade needs extra margin. And a lumped heat balance gives flows, not the cell-to-cell temperature spread, which needs cold-plate CFD and a propagation test.


Those steps take up most of a battery engineer's time. Skill-Lync's[Li-ion Battery System Design in EV and ES](https://skill-lync.com/electrical-engineering-courses/battery-system-design-ev-es-matlab) course covers series-parallel sizing, BMS and range estimation in MATLAB.[Battery Thermal Management using Ansys Fluent and MATLAB](https://skill-lync.com/electrical-engineering-courses/battery-thermal-management-system-ansys-fluent) takes the cooling step into CFD, and the[PG program in EV design and development](https://skill-lync.com/electrical-engineering-courses/masters-electric-vehicle-design-development) covers the whole vehicle. For pay in this field, see[EV engineer salaries](https://skill-lync.com/salaries/ev-engineer) .


## Frequently asked questions


### How do I calculate how many cells an EV battery pack needs?


Get the series count from the voltage window: maximum system voltage divided by the cell's full-charge voltage, checked against the minimum voltage. Get the parallel count from energy: pack energy divided by (series count × cell energy), rounded up. Then check per-cell current against the datasheet. For 40.3 kWh at 400 V class with 17.8 Wh cells, that is 96S24P, or 2,304 cells.


### Is a 400 V or an 800 V battery pack better?


At the same power, an 800 V pack carries half the current, so wiring losses are a quarter and fast charging is easier. It needs twice as many cells in series, a costlier inverter and parts rated for the higher voltage. For a cost-sensitive compact car, 400 V class is usually the simpler choice.


### Which standard does an Indian EV battery pack have to pass?


Cars, buses and trucks are type-approved to AIS-038 (Rev 2), and two- and three-wheelers to AIS-156, both as amended in 2022. Cells need IS 16893 Parts 2 and 3 certification from an NABL-accredited lab or a test agency notified under CMVR Rule 126.
